chunks: The enemies of the Sheikh did not cease in their persistent transgression; they used to exploit the masses to incite against him, until they burned his house, his books, and whatever he possessed of the chair of kalam (theology) and teaching.

key_terms.السَّوَادَ: the masses/common people — classical Arabic term (lit. 'the darkness/blackness') for the general populace of Iraq, here exploited as a tool for mob incitement
key_terms.تَمَادِيًا: persisting in excess — continuing beyond due bounds; a masdar used circumstantially to intensify the verb 'did not cease'
key_terms.طُغْيَانِهِمْ: their tyranny/transgression — exceeding all moral and legal limits; unbridled aggression
key_terms.كُرْسِيِّ الْكَلَامِ: chair of kalam — the prestigious academic seat of Islamic speculative theology from which the Sheikh formally lectured and debated

ai.seo_question: Why were Sheikh al-Tusi's house and books burned, and who incited the masses against him?
ai.summary: This passage describes the relentless persecution of Shaykh al-Tā'ifa Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṭūsī — the preeminent Shia jurist, hadith scholar, and theologian — by his adversaries in Baghdad. His opponents exploited the common populace to incite mob violence against him, ultimately burning his home, his library, and his prestigious academic seat. These events occurred around 448 AH during Seljuk-era sectarian tumult in Baghdad, compelling the Sheikh to emigrate permanently to Najaf al-Ashraf, where he established the enduring Shia scholarly tradition.
